module_title: Drying Specific Fruits: Mango, Banana, Pineapple, and More

lessons.title: Step-by-Step Drying of Mango Slices
lessons.body:
Choose firm, ripe mangoes that are sweet but not mushy. In Africa, varieties like Kent, Julie, or local mangoes work well. Wash them, peel with a sharp knife or peeler, and slice lengthwise into 1 cm thick slices. Remove the pit. To prevent browning, dip slices in a solution of 1 teaspoon ascorbic acid (or lemon juice) per 1 litre of water for 2 minutes. Drain well.

Pre-treat by blanching: bring water to 95Â°C, drop slices in for 2 minutes, then immediately transfer to cold water. This sets colour and speeds drying. Alternatively, syrup-blanch in a 30% sugar solution (300 g sugar per 1 litre water) for 3 minutes for sweeter, chewier slices.

Arrange slices in a single layer on drying trays. Use a solar dryer or electric dehydrator. Set temperature to 57-60Â°C. If using an oven, set to lowest setting (50-60Â°C) and prop door open 5 cm. Drying takes 6-10 hours. Turn slices every 2 hours. They are ready when leathery, pliable, and no moisture beads appear when squeezed.

Cool completely, then pack in airtight jars or vacuum-sealed bags. Store in a cool, dark place. Properly dried mango slices last 6-12 months. For a 10 kg fresh mango batch, you get about 1.5-2 kg dried slices. Sell in 100 g or 250 g packs. In many African markets, dried mango sells for 3-5 times the fresh price.

lessons.title: Making Sweet and Chewy Banana Chips
lessons.body:
Use firm, ripe but not overripe bananas. In East Africa, matoke or bogoya varieties are excellent. Peel and slice into 3-5 mm thick rounds or lengthwise strips. To keep them from browning, soak in 1 litre water with 1 tablespoon lemon juice for 10 minutes. Drain and pat dry.

For sweet and chewy chips, prepare a honey or sugar syrup: mix 250 g sugar or 200 ml honey with 500 ml water and 1 teaspoon cinnamon (optional). Bring to a boil, then add banana slices and simmer for 5 minutes. Remove and drain. This syrup infusion adds flavour and extends shelf life.

Dry at 55-60Â°C in a solar dryer or dehydrator for 8-12 hours. If using an oven, keep temperature at 50-60Â°C with door ajar. Turn chips every 2-3 hours. They are done when they bend without breaking and are dry to touch but still chewy. Over-drying makes them brittle.

Cool completely. Store in airtight containers. For 5 kg fresh bananas, you get about 1-1.5 kg chips. In Kenya, Uganda, and Nigeria, sweet banana chips are a popular snack. Package in 50 g or 100 g sealed bags. Add a desiccant packet if humidity is high. Sell to schools, supermarkets, and online. Shelf life is 6-9 months if stored properly.

lessons.title: Drying Pineapple Rings and Chunks
lessons.body:
Select ripe pineapples with a sweet aroma and golden skin. Remove top, base, and skin. Cut into 1 cm thick rings or 2 cm cubes. Remove eyes. For rings, core them. Soak in a solution of 1 teaspoon ascorbic acid per 1 litre water for 5 minutes to prevent browning.

Blanching is optional but recommended: dip in boiling water for 2 minutes, then cold water. This reduces drying time and preserves colour. For sweeter rings, blanch in light syrup (200 g sugar per 1 litre water) for 3 minutes.

Arrange on trays without overlapping. Dry at 55-60Â°C for 8-12 hours. Pineapple has high sugar and moisture, so it takes longer than mango. Turn every 2 hours. Rings are ready when leathery and pliable; chunks when springy but dry. In a solar dryer, it may take 1-2 days.

Cool and pack in airtight jars or vacuum bags. Store in a cool, dark place. From 10 kg fresh pineapple, you get about 1-1.5 kg dried product. Dried pineapple is a premium snack. In South Africa, Ghana, and Kenya, it sells well in health shops and export markets. You can also grind dried pineapple into powder for flavouring. Package in 100 g or 200 g bags. Shelf life is 9-12 months.

lessons.title: Drying Papaya, Guava, and Other Tropical Fruits
lessons.body:
Papaya: Choose ripe but firm papayas. Peel, cut in half, remove seeds, and slice into 1 cm thick strips or cubes. Papaya can be bland, so soak in light syrup (200 g sugar + 1 teaspoon citric acid per 1 litre water) for 30 minutes. Dry at 55-60Â°C for 6-10 hours until leathery. Papaya dries faster than mango. From 8 kg fresh, get 1-1.5 kg dried.

Guava: Use ripe but firm guavas. Wash, cut ends, and slice into 5 mm thick rounds or halves. Remove seeds if desired. Guava is high in pectin, so it dries chewy. No pre-treatment needed, but a 2-minute blanch helps. Dry at 55-60Â°C for 6-8 hours. From 5 kg fresh, get about 1 kg dried. Guava chips are popular in Kenya and Nigeria.

Other tropical fruits: Pawpaw (same as papaya), soursop (remove seeds, slice 1 cm, dry 8-10 hours), and jackfruit (use ripe pods, dry 10-12 hours). Mango, banana, and pineapple are covered in other lessons. For all, ensure they are dry enough: no moisture when squeezed. Cool completely before packing. Store in airtight containers. Use 100 g or 250 g packs. In African markets, dried tropical fruit mixes are growing in demand. Label with drying date and best before.

lessons.title: Drying Berries and Small Fruits Like Strawberries and Mulberries
lessons.body:
Berries are delicate and high in moisture. Use fresh, firm berries. Strawberries: hull and slice 5 mm thick. Mulberries: remove stems. Blueberries: blanch for 30 seconds to crack skins. For all, a 10-minute soak in 1 litre water with 1 tablespoon lemon juice helps preserve colour and vitamin C.

Dry at 50-55Â°C, lower than other fruits to prevent case hardening. Spread in a single layer on mesh trays. Drying takes 8-14 hours. Turn gently every 2 hours. They are ready when dry but still pliable, like raisins. Over-drying makes them hard. In humid African regions, use a dehydrator or solar dryer with good ventilation.

For 2 kg fresh strawberries, you get about 200-300 g dried. Mulberries yield similar. Pack in small airtight jars or vacuum bags. Add oxygen absorbers for longer shelf life. Store in cool, dark place. Dried berries are a premium product. Sell in 50 g or 100 g packs to health shops, bakeries, and hotels. In South Africa and Kenya, they fetch high prices. You can also mix with other dried fruits for trail mix. Shelf life is 6-12 months.

lessons.title: Flavoring Dried Fruits with Spices and Honey
lessons.body:
Flavoring dried fruits adds value and market appeal. Start with fully dried fruit (mango, banana, pineapple, etc.). For honey coating: warm 200 ml honey with 50 ml water and 1 teaspoon cinnamon or ginger. Dip dried fruit pieces for 2 minutes, then drain. Return to dryer at 50Â°C for 1-2 hours to set the coating. This makes them glossy and sweet.

Spice blends: For a savory-sweet mix, combine 2 tablespoons sugar, 1 teaspoon chili powder, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon citric acid. Toss dried fruit in this mix. For a tropical blend, use 1 tablespoon coconut sugar, 1/2 teaspoon nutmeg, and 1/2 teaspoon vanilla powder. For a tangy coating, mix 1 tablespoon tamarind paste with 1 tablespoon honey and brush on.

Ensure coated fruits are dried again to prevent spoilage. The honey or sugar coating can attract moisture, so pack with desiccant. Label clearly: "Honey-Cinnamon Mango" or "Spicy Pineapple." These value-added products sell for 20-50% more than plain dried fruit. In African markets, spiced dried fruits are popular in urban areas and for export. Experiment with local spices like cloves, cardamom, or hibiscus powder. Always test small batches first. Store in airtight containers in a cool, dark place. Shelf life remains 6-12 months if properly dried and packed.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Drying Specific Fruits â Mango, Banana, Pineapple, Papaya, Guava, Berries & Flavoured Blends

This practical reference is written for African agribusiness operators â small and medium processors, cooperatives, and women's groups â who want to turn surplus or low-grade fruit into shelf-stable, high-value dried products for local markets, urban supermarkets, and export. It consolidates the operational parameters you need across the six lessons in this module: mango slices, banana chips, pineapple rings and chunks, papaya and guava, berries and small fruits, and flavoured dried fruit blends. Treat it as your bench-side operating sheet.

The commercial logic is straightforward. Fresh mango, banana, and pineapple in most African production zones suffer 30â50% post-harvest losses during peak season, while dried fruit sells at a 3â8Ã value uplift per kilogram of fresh input. A processor who masters drying parameters â moisture content, temperature, pre-treatment, and hygiene â converts a perishable glut into a product with 6â12 months of shelf life, low transport cost, and access to regional and diaspora markets.

Core Drying Parameters by Fruit

The table below gives operating windows for the fruits covered in this module. These are practical ranges for cabinet, solar, and tunnel dryers in tropical conditions; adjust airflow and loading density to your equipment. Always confirm final moisture with a calibrated meter or the oven method before packing.

Table 1. Drying parameters for tropical fruits (cabinet / solar / tunnel dryers)
Fruit Preparation Pre-treatment Air temp (Â°C) Time (h) Final moisture
Mango (slices 5â8 mm) Peel, slice, remove fibre near stone 0.2% citric acid or 1% ascorbic dip, 3â5 min; or 30â40 Â°Brix sugar syrup 55â60 6â10 15â20%
Banana (chips 2â3 mm) Peel, slice crosswise or lengthwise Blanch 2â3 min; honey or syrup dip for sweet/chewy style 55â65 6â9 12â15%
Pineapple (rings 8â10 mm / chunks) Peel, core, slice or cube Blanch 2â4 min; 30â40 Â°Brix syrup for candied rings 55â60 8â12 15â18%
Papaya (cubes/slices) Peel, deseed, cube 10 mm Blanch 2 min; citric acid dip 55â60 8â12 15â18%
Guava (halves/slices) Wash, halve, remove seeds for slices Sugar syrup (30â40 Â°Brix) improves texture 55â60 8â12 15â18%
Strawberry / mulberry Whole or halved; berries are delicate Light syrup or honey dip; handle with trays to avoid crushing 50â55 8â14 12â18%

Sources: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 119, Fruit and Vegetable Processing (1995); FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius standards for dried fruits; and parameters compiled from the FAO Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing technical guides. Ranges are indicative for tropical ambient conditions (25â35 Â°C, 60â85% RH).

Yield, Value, and Business Planning

Before you buy a dryer, run the numbers. Dried fruit is a volume-reduction business: you need roughly 4â7 kg of fresh fruit to produce 1 kg of finished dried product, depending on fruit and final moisture. Your margin lives in the gap between farmgate price during glut season and the wholesale price of the dried product. The table below gives planning benchmarks for a small operation.

Table 2. Indicative fresh-to-dried conversion and value benchmarks (small-scale processing)
Fruit Fresh : dried ratio Peak-season farmgate (indicative) Dried wholesale (indicative) Key market
Mango 5â6 : 1 Low during glut 3â8Ã fresh value / kg Urban supermarkets, export, diaspora
Banana 4â5 : 1 Very low; high waste 4â6Ã fresh value / kg Snack retail, schools, kiosks
Pineapple 6â8 : 1 Low; processing culls cheap 5â8Ã fresh value / kg Confectionery, export, hotels
Papaya / guava 6â8 : 1 Low; often unsold 4â7Ã fresh value / kg Health food, local blends
Berries (strawberry, mulberry) 7â10 : 1 Seasonal, fragile Premium 6â10Ã fresh value / kg Specialty, wellness, export

Sources: Ratios and value multipliers are indicative planning benchmarks drawn from FAO Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing guides, ITC market briefs on dried tropical fruit, and typical West/East African processing cooperative data. Actual prices vary by country, season, and quality grade â always verify with current local market surveys before committing capital.

Flavouring Dried Fruits with Spices and Honey

Flavoured dried fruit is where small African processors differentiate and capture premium margins. The technique is simple: infuse before drying, or coat after drying. For honey-glazed banana chips, dip blanched slices in a 1:1 honey-water solution (pasteurised honey, 60 Â°C) for 10â15 minutes, drain, then dry at 55â60 Â°C. For spiced mango, dust with a blend of chilli, ginger, cinnamon, and a little salt after the fruit reaches 20% moisture, then return to the dryer for 30â60 minutes to set the coating. Always use food-grade spices and declare allergens (honey is not suitable for infants under 12 months â label accordingly).

Honey infusion adds sugars that bind water, so expect a slightly higher final moisture (up to 20%) and a shorter shelf life unless you use airtight packaging with a desiccant or vacuum seal. Test small batches, record your recipe, and keep a sensory log so you can reproduce winning flavours at scale.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Sulphites and Hygiene

Do not use sulphur fumigation or sulphite dips unless you are trained, licensed, and able to declare sulphites on the label. Sulphite residues above legal limits (typically 500â2,000 mg/kg depending on product and market) can trigger severe reactions in asthmatics and are restricted in the EU and many export markets. For most African small-scale operations, citric acid, ascorbic acid, blanching, and good hygiene are safer and sufficient. Always wash hands, sanitise trays, use potable water, and dry at temperatures that kill pathogens (â¥55 Â°C surface temperature) while preventing recontamination during cooling and packing.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Select and grade: Use ripe but firm fruit; reject mouldy, bruised, or over-ripe fruit before peeling.
  • Wash and sanitise: Use potable water; sanitise knives, trays, and drying racks between batches.
  • Pre-treat: Blanch or dip in citric/ascorbic acid to prevent browning and extend shelf life.
  • Uniform sizing: Cut slices to consistent thickness (5â10 mm) so all pieces dry at the same rate.
  • Control temperature: Hold 55â60 Â°C for most fruits; never exceed 70 Â°C or you get case-hardening.
  • Ensure airflow: Load trays no more than 1â2 kg/mÂ² and leave gaps for air movement.
  • Test moisture: Confirm 15â20% (or product-specific target) with a moisture meter or oven method before packing.
  • Cool and pack: Cool fully in a dry, clean room; pack in airtight, food-grade, moisture-barrier bags with a label showing date, batch, and allergens.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Fruit and Vegetable Processing (Agricultural Services Bulletin 119)
  • FAO â Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â Standards for Dried and Processed Fruits
  • Institute of Food Science & Technology â Food Processing Resources
  • International Trade Centre â Market Briefs on Dried Tropical Fruit

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Dried Fruit & Vegetable Processing. Verify all parameters against your local regulations and equipment manufacturer guidance before commercial production.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for mango slices before drying?
quiz.explanation: 1 cm thick slices dry evenly and produce a good texture.

quiz.q: Why are mango slices dipped in ascorbic acid or lemon juice before drying?
quiz.explanation: Ascorbic acid or lemon juice inhibits enzymatic browning.

quiz.q: What temperature range is best for drying mango slices?
quiz.explanation: 57-60Â°C is ideal for safe and efficient drying without cooking the fruit.

quiz.q: How can you tell when mango slices are fully dried?
options: A) They are hard and brittle
B) They are leathery and pliable
quiz.explanation: Leathery and pliable with no moisture beads indicates proper drying.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield of dried mango from 10 kg fresh mango?
quiz.explanation: Fresh mango has high water content, so yield is about 15-20%.

quiz.q: Which banana variety is recommended for making sweet and chewy chips?
options: B) Firm, ripe bananas like matoke
quiz.explanation: Firm, ripe bananas hold shape and give chewy texture.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of soaking banana slices in lemon water?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice prevents enzymatic browning.

quiz.q: What temperature should be used for drying banana chips?
quiz.explanation: 55-60Â°C dries evenly without making them brittle.

quiz.q: How long does it take to dry banana chips in a dehydrator?
quiz.explanation: 8-12 hours at 55-60Â°C is typical for chewy chips.

quiz.q: What is a key sign that banana chips are done?
options: A) They are hard and break easily
quiz.explanation: Chewy chips bend without breaking; brittle means over-dried.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for pineapple rings?
quiz.explanation: 1 cm rings dry evenly and are easy to handle.

quiz.q: Why is blanching recommended for pineapple before drying?
options: B) To reduce drying time and preserve colour
quiz.explanation: Blanching sets colour and speeds up drying.

quiz.q: How long does pineapple take to dry compared to mango?
quiz.explanation: Pineapple has high sugar and moisture, so it takes longer.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield of dried pineapple from 10 kg fresh?
quiz.explanation: Pineapple has high water content, yielding about 10-15% dried.

quiz.q: How can dried pineapple be used besides as a snack?
options: B) Ground into powder for flavouring
quiz.explanation: Dried pineapple can be ground into powder for various uses.

quiz.q: What pre-treatment is recommended for papaya before drying?
options: B) Soak in light syrup with citric acid
quiz.explanation: Syrup with citric acid improves flavour and colour.

quiz.q: How long does guava take to dry at 55-60Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Guava dries relatively quickly due to its texture.

quiz.q: What is a common characteristic of dried guava?
quiz.explanation: Guava's high pectin makes it chewy when dried.

quiz.q: Which of these is a tropical fruit that can be dried?
quiz.explanation: Soursop is a tropical fruit suitable for drying.

quiz.q: What should you do before packing any dried fruit?
quiz.explanation: Cooling prevents condensation and spoilage.

quiz.q: Why are berries dried at a lower temperature (50-55Â°C)?
quiz.explanation: Lower temperature prevents outer skin from drying too fast.

quiz.q: What pre-treatment helps strawberries retain colour?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice (ascorbic acid) preserves colour and vitamin C.

quiz.q: How long does it take to dry strawberries?
quiz.explanation: 8-14 hours at 50-55Â°C is typical for strawberries.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield of dried strawberries from 2 kg fresh?
quiz.explanation: Strawberries have high water content, yielding about 10-15%.

quiz.q: What should be added to packed dried berries to extend shelf life?
quiz.explanation: Oxygen absorbers reduce oxidation and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a good way to add flavour to dried fruits?
options: B) Coat with honey and spices
quiz.explanation: Honey and spice coatings add value and taste.

quiz.q: After coating dried fruit with honey, what should you do?
options: B) Dry again at 50Â°C for 1-2 hours
quiz.explanation: Re-drying sets the coating and prevents moisture.

quiz.q: Which spice is commonly used in sweet dried fruit coatings?
quiz.explanation: Cinnamon is popular for sweet coatings.

quiz.q: How much more can flavoured dried fruits sell for compared to plain?
quiz.explanation: Value-added products command higher prices.

quiz.q: Why should flavoured dried fruits be packed with desiccant?
quiz.explanation: Honey and sugar coatings attract moisture; desiccant keeps them dry.
